power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Diabetes is an increasing public health challenge in India, particularly among middle-aged and older adults.
Understanding its prevalence and associated risk factors is essential for informing prevention and management strategies.

Objective: This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of diabetes and identify demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, and health-related factors associated with diabetes among adults aged 45 years and above in India.

A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using nationally representative data from the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) Wave-1 (2017-18), comprising 72,055 individuals aged 45 years and above.
Diabetes status was based on respondents' self-reported diagnosis by a health professional.

Descriptive statistics were used to estimate diabetes prevalence, and multivariable binary logistic regression was performed to examine associations between diabetes and selected covariates, including age group, sex, place of residence, caste, religion, physical activity, dietary practices, heart disease, and heart attack risk.
Results: Diabetes prevalence was higher among older adults, urban residents, females, and individuals belonging to the Other Backward Classes (OBC).

After adjustment for potential confounders, age, urban residence, caste, religion, heart disease, and heart attack risk were significantly associated with diabetes, whereas sex was not statistically significant after adjustment.
Individuals aged 55-64 years and those residing in urban areas exhibited significantly higher odds of diabetes compared with their respective reference groups.
Conclusions: Diabetes is highly prevalent among middle-aged and older adults in India and is associated with several demographic, socioeconomic, and health-related factors.

These findings highlight population groups that may benefit from targeted prevention, screening, and NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice. management strategies.
Further longitudinal studies are warranted to clarify temporal relationships and causal pathways.

Diabetes mellitus is one of the fastest-growing non-communicable diseases worldwide and represents a major public health challenge because of its increasing prevalence, long-term complications, and substantial economic burden.
The International Diabetes Federation estimates that more than 537 million adults were living with diabetes in 2021, with this number projected to increase markedly over the coming decades.
Low-and middle-income countries account for most of this increase, reflecting rapid population ageing, urbanisation, and lifestyle transitions (Bjork & Stefan (2003), Anjana et al., 2011).

text.text: India has one of the largest populations of people living with diabetes.

Rapid demographic change, urbanisation, reduced physical activity, dietary transitions, and increasing obesity have contributed to a substantial rise in diabetes prevalence over recent decades (Hu F. B., 2011).

text.text: However, relatively few studies have comprehensively examined the combined influence of demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, and health-related characteristics among middle-aged and older adults using data from the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI).

Given India's rapidly ageing population, identifying population groups with a higher prevalence of diabetes is important for planning prevention and disease management strategies (Wanga. Et al., 2018 and Wong E. et al., 2013).

text.text: Therefore, the present study aims to estimate the prevalence of diabetes among adults aged 45 years and above in India and to examine its association with demographic (age, sex, place of residence, caste, and religion), behavioural (physical activity and dietary practices), and healthrelated factors (heart disease and heart attack history) using nationally representative LASI Wave-1 (2017-18) data through multivariable binary logistic regression analysis.

Some key areas of research and Literature on Condition of Diabetes in India include: -Diabetes is the most common non-communicable disease globally.
The estimated number of adults with diabetes in 2007 was 246 million of these, 80% live in developing countries, the largest numbers on the Indian subcontinent and in China.
Approximately 85-95% of all cases of diabetes are type 2 diabetes and the worldwide explosion of this disorder is a major health care burden.
It is estimated that nearly 380 million adults worldwide will have diabetes by 2025.
India has 41 million diabetics, and this number is expected to increase to 70 million by 2025.

The increased number of diabetics in India is likely to be due to a significant increase in the incidence of type 2 diabetes, caused by unprecedented rates of urbanization, which results in environmental and lifestyle changes (Krishnan.A. et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The increased number of diabetics in India is likely to be due to a significant increase in the incidence of type 2 diabetes, caused by unprecedented rates of urbanization, which results in environmental and lifestyle changes <ref type="bibr">(Krishnan.A. et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: According to World Health Organization (WHO) estimates, the urban population in developing regions will increase from 1.9 billion in 2000 to 3.9 billion in 2030.
It is estimated that, by 2030, nearly 46% of India's population will be living in urban areas.
Chronic diseases, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease (CVD), pose a primary challenge for the health care system.
India is the second most populous country, with considerable diversity in caste, religion, habitat, and socioeconomic status, lifestyle, and food habits.

Although several infectious and parasitic diseases have been controlled successfully in India, non-communicable diseases are becoming increasingly common, resulting in an enormous burden on the health care system.
Significant economic improvements have occurred in India, but the large population creates difficulties for the effective reduction of poverty, malnutrition, and the provision of health care to all.
India, China, and Pakistan contribute 21%, 12%, and 5%, respectively, to the annual increase in the global population (Ramachandran Ambady, 2012).

text.text: India, a country experiencing rapid socioeconomic progress and urbanization, carries a considerable share of the global diabetes burden.

Studies in different parts of India have demonstrated an escalating prevalence of diabetes not only in urban populations, but also in rural populations because of the urbanization of lifestyle parameters (Tandon, N. et al., 2018).

Diabetes is Major Cause of Blindness, kidney failure, Heart attacks, stroke and lower limb amputation.

text.text: Diabetes is a severe chronic disease that arises when insulin generation is insufficient, or the generated insulin cannot be used in the body, resulting a long-term metabolic disorder.
Diabetes affects an estimated 537 million adults worldwide between the ages of 20 and 79 (10.5% of all adults in this age range).
By 2030, 643 million people will have diabetes globally, increasing to 783 million by 2045.

According to the IDF 10th edition, the incidence of diabetes has been rising in Southeast Asia (SEA) nations for at least 20 years, and current estimates have outperformed all previous forecasts (Kumar Arvind, 2024).

>Methodology

text.text: This study is a cross-sectional secondary analysis of data obtained from the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) Wave-1 (2017-18).
Although LASI is a longitudinal cohort study, the present analysis uses only the baseline survey; therefore, all findings are based on cross-sectional data.

LASI is a nationally representative survey conducted by the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, and several international partners.

The survey collected detailed information on demographic characteristics, socioeconomic conditions, physical and mental health, healthcare utilisation, chronic diseases, and health-related behaviours among adults aged 45 years and above and their spouses across all states and union territories of India.
The present study included 72,055 respondents aged 45 years and above with complete information on diabetes status and selected explanatory variables.
Individuals with missing information on the outcome or key covariates were excluded from the multivariable analysis.
The outcome variable was self-reported diabetes mellitus.

Respondents were classified as having diabetes if they answered "Yes" to the LASI question asking whether a doctor or other health professional had ever diagnosed them with diabetes or high blood sugar.
The outcome variable was coded as:

Based on previous epidemiological studies and the availability of variables in LASI, the following explanatory variables were included in the analysis: • Age group (<45, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, and ≥75 years) • Sex (Male/Female) • Place of residence (Rural/Urban) • Caste (SC, ST, OBC, Others) • Religion (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Others) • Physical activity (Daily, Weekly, Never)

text.text: If respondents younger than 45 years were retained because they were spouses of age-eligible participants, this has been explicitly acknowledged.
Otherwise, this category should be excluded from all analyses to maintain consistency with the stated study population.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the characteristics of the study population and estimate the prevalence of diabetes across demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, and healthrelated characteristics.
Pearson's chi-square test was used to assess bivariate associations between diabetes status and categorical explanatory variables.
Multivariable binary logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with diabetes.
Variables included in the adjusted model were selected based on previous epidemiological evidence and their established relevance to diabetes.
Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated.
Statistical significance was assessed at a two-sided p < 0.05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was assessed at a two-sided p < 0.05.

text.text: All analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (Version XX).
Data management and figure preparation were conducted using Microsoft Excel.
This study used publicly available, de-identified LASI Wave-1 data.

Ethical approval for data collection was obtained by the LASI investigators from the Institutional Review Board of the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai, and informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection.
Since the present study involved secondary analysis of anonymized data, no additional ethical approval was required.
Table 3.1 presents the baseline characteristics of the 72,055 adults aged 45 years and above included in the analysis.
Overall, 11.6% of participants reported having been diagnosed with diabetes.
Diabetes prevalence increased with age and was highest among participants aged 65-74 years, followed by those aged 55-64 years.
The prevalence was higher among women, urban residents, participants belonging to the Other Backward Class (OBC) category, and
Christians.
Significant differences in diabetes prevalence were also observed according to physical activity, special diet, heart disease, and heart attack history (all p < 0.05).

text.text: After adjusting for potential confounding variables, age, place of residence, caste, religion, heart disease, and heart attack history remained significantly associated with diabetes.

Compared with the reference group, adults aged 55-64 years had 2.40 times higher odds of diabetes (AOR = 2.40; 95% CI: 1.22-4.71), while those aged 65-74 years had the highest odds (AOR = 2.48; 95% CI: 1.26-4.88).
Adults aged 75 years and above also had significantly greater odds of diabetes (AOR = 2.27; 95% CI: 1.13-4.55), indicating an increasing likelihood of diabetes with advancing age.
Urban residence was independently associated with diabetes.
Participants living in urban areas had more than twice the odds of diabetes compared with those living in rural areas (AOR = 2.30; 95% CI: 1.92-2.76).

With respect to social characteristics, respondents belonging to the Other Backward Class (OBC) had significantly higher odds of diabetes than those from the Scheduled Caste category (AOR = 1.53; 95% CI: 1.14-2.05).
Similarly, Christian participants had higher odds of diabetes than Hindu participants (AOR = 1.69; 95% CI: 1.18-2.44).

The present study examined the prevalence of diabetes and its associated demographic, socioeconomic, and health-related factors among adults aged 45 years and above in India using nationally representative data from LASI Wave-1 (2017-18).
Overall, approximately one in nine participants reported having diabetes, highlighting the substantial burden of the disease among middle-aged and older adults in India.
The multivariable analysis demonstrated that increasing age was significantly associated with higher odds of diabetes.
Adults aged 55 years and above had greater odds of diabetes than those aged 45-54 years, with the highest odds observed among individuals aged 65-74 years.

This age-related pattern is consistent with previous Indian studies using LASI and other national datasets, which have reported that diabetes prevalence increases with age because of progressive metabolic changes, longer exposure to behavioural risk factors, and population ageing.
Similar findings have also been reported in studies based on the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) and other epidemiological investigations conducted in India.
Urban residence was independently associated with higher odds of diabetes.
Participants living in urban areas had more than twice the odds of diabetes compared with rural residents.

This finding is consistent with earlier evidence from India, where urban populations generally experience greater exposure to sedentary lifestyles, dietary transitions, obesity, and other cardiometabolic risk factors.
However, the present study cannot determine whether urban residence itself causes diabetes because the analysis is based on cross-sectional observational data.
The analysis also identified socioeconomic differences in diabetes prevalence.

Participants belonging to the Other Backward Class (OBC) had significantly higher odds of diabetes than those from the Scheduled Caste category, while Christian participants showed higher odds than Hindus after adjustment for other variables.
These findings may reflect differences in socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviours, healthcare utilisation, and regional variation.
However, the present analysis did not directly examine these mechanisms; therefore, these associations should be interpreted cautiously.
Heart disease and previous heart attack were significantly associated with diabetes in the adjusted model.
Because the outcome and covariates were measured at the same time, the temporal relationship between these conditions cannot be established.
Consequently, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that heart disease or heart attack reduces or increases the risk of diabetes.

Instead, they likely reflect the complex coexistence of chronic diseases among older adults and may also be influenced by residual confounding, treatment effects, or differences in healthcare utilisation.
Contrary to the unadjusted descriptive findings, sex was not significantly associated with diabetes after adjustment for other covariates.
Likewise, no statistically significant associations were observed for Scheduled Tribe (ST) or Muslim participants after controlling for potential confounders.
These findings suggest that demographic and socioeconomic factors, particularly age and place of residence, explain a substantial proportion of the observed variation in diabetes prevalence.
The findings of this study should be interpreted in light of several limitations.
First, the analysis is based on cross-sectional baseline data from LASI Wave-1; therefore, causal relationships cannot be inferred.
Second, diabetes status was based on self-reported physician diagnosis, which may underestimate the true prevalence because undiagnosed cases were not captured.
Third, information on dietary intake, medication adherence, duration of diabetes, glycaemic control, and several behavioural risk factors was not comprehensively examined in the present analysis.
Despite these limitations, the study benefits from the use of a large, nationally representative sample, allowing the findings to be generalised to the Indian population aged 45 years and above.

Overall, the findings identify important demographic and socioeconomic groups with a higher prevalence of diabetes and provide evidence that may assist in prioritising screening and preventive strategies among middle-aged and older adults.
However, further longitudinal analyses using subsequent waves of LASI are required to examine temporal relationships and better understand the progression of diabetes over time.

The multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that increasing age, urban residence, Other Backward Class (OBC) status, and Christian religion were independently associated with higher odds of diabetes after adjusting for potential confounding factors.
In contrast, sex and several other sociodemographic characteristics were not significantly associated with diabetes after adjustment.
These findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal relationships, as the analysis was based on cross-sectional baseline data from LASI.
Furthermore, diabetes status was based on self-reported physician diagnosis, which may underestimate the true prevalence because undiagnosed cases were not captured.
Consequently, the temporal relationship between diabetes and the associated factors cannot be established.
Despite these limitations, the study provides nationally representative evidence on demographic and socioeconomic disparities in diabetes among middle-aged and older adults in India.
The findings may help identify population groups that could benefit from targeted diabetes screening and prevention initiatives.

Future research using longitudinal follow-up data from subsequent LASI waves is needed to investigate temporal changes and better understand the causal pathways underlying diabetes among older adults in India.
